claims.text: Conventional casting of CoCrFeNiTi yields a porous, soft, single-phase FCC structure with hardness below 200 HV.
Slow cooling or aging of CoCrFeNiTi can produce HCP phases.
High-energy milling at about 400 rpm for 4–6 h with intermittent cooling is an appropriate powder-processing regime.
SPS should be performed at 1050–1100 °C, 30–50 MPa, with a heating rate above 50 °C/min, a dwell below 5 min, and rapid cooling.
Rapid thermal expansion and pressure application create a high strain rate during sintering.
High-energy milling followed by rapid SPS will suppress porosity in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed process will produce grains below 500 nm and a solid solution dominated by FCC with a minor BCC fraction.
Rapid SPS will suppress Ti-rich HCP and Laves-phase formation.
A short sintering time limits Ti segregation and diffusion-controlled formation of HCP or Laves phases.
Defects and grain boundaries introduced by milling act as nucleation sites for the FCC solid solution.
High heating rate and applied pressure densify the alloy before phase decomposition can occur.
High configurational entropy and rapid quenching enhance FCC stability.
The processed alloy will exceed 400 HV and be significantly harder than cast CoCrFeNiTi.
The hardness increase will arise from both grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening.
Suppressing HCP phases will avoid the brittleness associated with those phases.
Ti-rich HCP phases become thermodynamically stable above a threshold likely greater than 1150 °C.
Ti contents above about 15 at.% may cause HCP formation despite rapid processing.
A sample treated at 1150 °C for 30 min should have more HCP phase and lower hardness than one treated at 1050 °C for 5 min.
Vickers hardness should be measured at a 500 g load with a 15 s dwell.
The hypothesis is falsified if the 1050 °C/5 min sample has more than 10% HCP, more than 5% porosity, or hardness below 300 HV.

contradictions.description: The operating hypothesis requires a dwell time strictly below 5 min, but the principal test sample is held for exactly 5 min.

The predicted hardness target is above 400 HV, whereas the falsification rule rejects only hardness below 300 HV; results from 300 to 400 HV would miss the stated target without falsifying the hypothesis.
The predicted material is described as fully consolidated, but the falsification rule permits as much as 5% porosity.
